Drawn out, or born?

Three letters, one verse, and about two thousand years of argument over where the name מֹשֶׁה Moshe comes from. This time you do not have to take anyone's word for it. Weigh the evidence, compare the sounds, read the manuscripts, and set your own odds against ours.

01 / 13 The verse
    01 · Exodus 2:10

    The Torah's own explanation

    וַתִּקְרָא שְׁמוֹ מֹשֶׁה וַתֹּאמֶר כִּי מִן־הַמַּיִם מְשִׁיתִהוּ

    She called his name Moshe, and she said: for out of the water I drew him.

    Pharaoh's daughter names the infant she pulled from the Nile

    Exodus tells it in a few lines. A Levite mother hides her son from Pharaoh's decree and sets him in a basket among the Nile reeds. Pharaoh's daughter finds him, and his own mother is brought in to nurse him. Then the princess names him, and the verse gives her reason.

    The reason is a Hebrew pun. The name is tied to the verb מ־ש־ה (m-sh-h), "to draw out." It is one of the rarest verbs in the Bible, and every time it appears, water is involved. The explorer below shows each place it occurs, including a possible echo in Isaiah.

    Two problems have bothered readers for centuries. The first is grammar. The form of the name does not match the baby's role in the story. The second is the speaker. Why would an Egyptian princess name a child with a Hebrew pun? Almost every theory on this page is an answer to one of those two questions. Take the verse apart below and compare the name with the verb the princess uses.

    Exodus 2:10 word by word, with the three forms of the verb m-sh-h.

    Traditional readers turned the snag into the point. The boy drawn from the water would be the one who draws Israel out of Egypt and through the sea. Midrash HaGadol says the princess chose the name knowing that. Modern scholars read the same mismatch as a sign that the verse explains an older name after the fact. Even Thomas Schneider, who argues the name is Hebrew, concedes that the verse's own explanation does not really work as grammar.

    02 · Every proposal on record

    The theories, scored

    There are two serious answers and a handful of others. The Semitic answer says the name is Hebrew, or at least West Semitic, and that the verse is roughly right about the root. The Egyptian answer says the name is the Egyptian ms, "born" or "child," the same element found in Thutmose, Ahmose and Ramesses. Karl Lepsius proposed it in 1849, and BDB, the standard Hebrew lexicon, still calls it probable.

    Neither side has a knockout. Each has a few strong arguments and a few weak ones, and how you rank them depends on what kind of evidence you trust. Below, each theory has its own card. Move the weights to match your judgment and watch the odds change. Your result stays in this browser, and the verdict at the end of the page sets it beside ours.

    A scorecard of the theories of the name's origin, with adjustable evidence weights.

    Real Egyptians called Mose

    The Egyptian theory has real people behind it. A scribe of the treasury of Ptah named Mose lived under Ramesses II. His tomb chapel near Memphis records a land lawsuit that began with a grant under Ahmose I. His mother Nubnofret lost the case in Year 18 of Ramesses II, and Mose reopened it. Nobody proposes him as Moses, but he proves that a bare "Mose" was a real name. The most serious attempt to find the man himself is Rolf Krauss's. He argued that the biblical writer modeled Moses on Amenmesse, a rival king of about 1203–1200 BCE whose name one papyrus writes simply as "Msy." The Egyptologist Aidan Dodson called the idea "intriguing, but beyond proof."

    Moses is also not the only Levite with an Egyptian-looking name. Phinehas, from pꜣ-nḥsj, "the Nubian," is close to consensus. Hophni may be an Egyptian word for "tadpole." Hur, Merari, Miriam and Aaron have been proposed too, but each is contested. Richard Elliott Friedman argues that only the Levites carry such names, and concludes that the Levites were the group that came out of Egypt. One critic replies that priestly families could have picked up Egyptian names in Canaan, which Egypt ruled until the 12th century BCE.

    03 · Why the Egyptian theory is wobbling

    The sound problem

    For most of the twentieth century the Egyptian derivation was the textbook answer. Freud built Moses and Monotheism (1939) on it, quoting the historian James Breasted that the name was simply the Egyptian word for "child." Freud then said he could not take responsibility for the details. In 2023, and again on TheTorah.com in August 2026, the Egyptologist Thomas Schneider of the University of British Columbia set out why the sounds do not line up.

    His case has four parts: the consonant, the vowels, the stress, and a long silence. The ancient writers who knew Egyptian names ending in -mose never connected them to Moses. The lab below lets you compare each piece, period by period, and test it against other Egyptian words that came into Hebrew.

    The stakes are larger than one name. Rudolf Smend argued that Israel would not invent an Egyptian name for its founder, so an Egyptian Moshe would be evidence that the tradition really comes out of Egypt. If the name is Semitic, that argument disappears.

    The Egyptian and Hebrew forms of the name compared sound by sound, with the Shibboleth test.

    Could his lisp explain it?

    A reader asked us whether Moses' own speech impediment could explain why an Egyptian s became a Hebrew sh. The tradition of the impediment is real, and the lab sets it out. The short answer is no. Other people wrote and used his name, so his own pronunciation cannot account for the spelling, and it would leave the vowels and the stress untouched.

    The stronger form of the idea is about dialects, and the Shibboleth story in Judges 12 supplies it. Hebrew speakers themselves did not agree on s and sh. That loosens the consonant objection. It does nothing for the vowels or the stress.

    04 · Sargon, Horus and the exposed child

    The child in the basket

    Moses is one of many heroes abandoned at birth and raised by strangers. The closest match is older than Israel. Sargon of Akkad ruled about 2334–2279 BCE, and scribes of the 8th and 7th centuries BCE copied a first-person legend of his birth. His mother, a high priestess, bore him in secret, sealed him in a reed basket with bitumen and set him on the river. Akki, the drawer of water, lifted him out while dipping his bucket and raised him as his son.

    The parallel may reach the name itself. If Moshe means "the one who draws out," the Hebrew hero carries the title of Sargon's rescuer, and scholars from Otto Rank to John Huddlestun have asked whether that is a coincidence. Compare the two stories line by line below, then see where Moses sits among the other exposed infants.

    Sargon's birth legend and Exodus 2 side by side, with a table of other exposed-infant heroes.

    Egypt has its own version. Isis hid the infant Horus from Set in the papyrus marshes of the Delta. Gary Rendsburg treats this as the closest parallel of all. Both mothers hide a son among Delta reeds, and both stories dwell on nursing. Since Pharaoh was the living Horus, the story quietly makes Moses Pharaoh's equal.

    Moses also breaks the pattern. No prophecy announces him, and no parent wants him dead. His mother sets him afloat to escape a decree and watches over the basket.

    05 · Manuscripts and translations

    What the scribes wrote

    The letters of the name were never quite fixed. The Masoretic text, the standard Hebrew text of the Bible, writes it with three letters, משה. Scribes at Qumran often wrote מושה, adding a vav for the o. Greek translators had no letter for sh and wrote it their own way. In one verse of Judges the name was changed by a single raised letter. Rashi explains that scribes did it to protect Moses' honour, while the Talmud (Bava Batra 109b) gives a different reason. Open the manuscripts below and compare the witnesses.

    The name in the Masoretic text, the Dead Sea Scrolls and the Septuagint, and the suspended nun of Judges 18:30.

    What the pagans called him

    Outside Jewish scripture, writers argued about who Moses was and gave him other names. Manetho, an Egyptian priest of the early 3rd century BCE quoted by Josephus, said a rebel priest of Heliopolis called Osarseph changed his name to Moses. Chaeremon, Nero's tutor, gave him the Egyptian name Tisithen. Strabo called him an Egyptian priest.

    The Jewish writer Artapanus turned the charge around in the 2nd century BCE. His Moses was the Greeks' Mousaios, teacher of Orpheus, and the Egyptian priests named him Hermes for interpreting the sacred letters. The Platonist Numenius called him Musaeus, and asked what Plato was but "Moses speaking Attic Greek." All of them made Moses an Egyptian or a Greek hero. None of them derived his name from the Egyptian ms.

    06 · Midrash and the medieval commentators

    Ten names, one chosen

    The rabbis gave Pharaoh's daughter a name of her own. They called her Bithiah, בִּתְיָה, "daughter of God," drawing on 1 Chronicles 4:18. The midrash says Moses was called by many names, each given by a different person, though the sources do not agree on the list. In Leviticus Rabbah 1:3, God tells him that of all of them He will use only the one Bithiah gave. Exodus Rabbah 1:26 makes the same point, and that is why the Torah never calls him anything else. Meet the ten names of Leviticus Rabbah below.

    The ten names the midrash gives Moses, and who gave each one.

    Five answers to the princess problem

    The commentators still had to explain how an Egyptian princess came up with a Hebrew pun. They found five ways out.

    • She learned Hebrew. Chizkuni gives this as his first reading, and Ibn Ezra allows it too.
    • His mother named him. Chizkuni's second reading, and Abravanel's. Jocheved gave the name, and the princess kept it because it fit.
    • It is a translation. Ibn Ezra says his Egyptian name was Munius and the Torah rendered it into Hebrew. His source, the Nabatean Agriculture, does not appear to contain it. Schneider's own guess is an Egyptian mou-nes, "water-cast."
    • An Egyptian name, retold in Hebrew. Philo and Josephus in antiquity, and Shadal and David Zvi Hoffmann in the 19th century.
    • He had another Hebrew name. Pseudo-Philo calls him Melchiel, and Clement of Alexandria calls him Joachim.
    07 · Numerical value

    345 and other numbers

    Every Hebrew letter is also a number, and Moshe comes to 345: mem 40, shin 300, he 5. The rabbis read totals like this as hints. The Talmud (Chullin 139b) asks where Moses is hinted at in the Torah and points to the word בְּשַׁגַּם in Genesis 6:3. Bereshit Rabbah 26:6 spells out the arithmetic. The word has the same value as Moshe, and the same verse sets a human lifespan at 120 years, the age Moses reached.

    Later readers kept finding matches. Some are classical, from the Talmud and midrash. Some are medieval, from Baal HaTurim or the manuscript Rabbi Kasher cites. Others are modern, popular or Samaritan. The lab marks which is which. Type any Hebrew word to see its value.

    A gematria calculator, with the words and names that share Moshe's value.

    08 · Across languages

    One name, many mouths

    English Moses comes through Greek. The Septuagint wrote Mōusēs, with the sh written as s and the final -s usual in Greek men's names. Latin took it from there. Arabic Mūsā came through Syriac. Follow the branches below.

    A family tree of the name's forms across languages.

    In each new place the name was reshaped. Jewish immigrants to America mostly set it aside for an American name, and the tree shows which one most of them chose.

    English turned the name into an oath, "Oh, Moses" by 1840 and "Holy Moses" by 1877, and into an adjective. Mosaic, "of Moses," dates from the 1660s. Mosaic the art form is older, from about 1400, and comes from Medieval Latin musaicum, "work of the Muses." The two words share no root.

    The titles differ by tradition. The Bible calls him "man of God" and "servant of the LORD." The title Moshe Rabbenu, "Moses our teacher," never appears in the Mishnah, though it is common in the Babylonian Talmud. In Islam Musa is Kalīm Allāh, "the one who conversed with God," after Quran 4:164.

    The name is on the map too. Yemin Moshe in Jerusalem, built in 1892–94, takes its name from Moses Montefiore and from Isaiah 63:12. Wadi Musa, the Valley of Moses, is the town at the gate of Petra.

    09 · Chronology

    4,000 years on one line

    The argument is easier to follow in order. Sargon's legend is older than any text about Moses. The Egyptian names in -mose belong to the Late Bronze Age. The Greek translators, Philo and Josephus come more than a thousand years later. Champollion read hieroglyphs in 1822, and in 1849 Lepsius proposed the Egyptian ms etymology. Move along the line below, or jump between eras.

    A dated timeline of the name, from Sargon of Akkad to 2026.

    Many of these dates are approximate, and the date of Exodus 2 itself is debated. Most scholars place the writing of the Pentateuch between about 600 and 400 BCE. Others tie the birth story to the reign of Hezekiah, in the late 8th century.

    10 · Who carried the name

    The great avoidance, then everywhere

    For most of antiquity, Jews did not name their sons Moses. In 1997 the papyrologist Tomasz Derda searched the Greek papyri and the Jewish inscriptions for people called Moses. He found no ancient document in which a bearer of the name can be securely identified as Jewish.

    The first men called Moses outside the Bible were Christians in Egypt. The name turns up in papyri of the early 4th century CE, and by about 350 CE it is common, mostly among clergy and monks. Moses the Black, the Desert Father, belongs to this wave.

    Jewish sources know just one exception, a layman mentioned once in the Babylonian Talmud. No rabbi of the Mishnah or the Talmud bears the name. The first clearly attested Jewish Moshes are rabbis of the 9th and 10th centuries. Moses Kahana ben Jacob led the academy of Sura from 825 or 832, and Moses ben Hanokh, who died about 965, taught in Córdoba.

    The likeliest reason is reverence. Derda compares it to the Christian avoidance of the name Jesus. Muslims felt no such restraint. Musa ibn Nusayr, born about 640, oversaw the conquest of Iberia.

    Then the dam broke. When Israel was founded, Moshe was the most common name for Jewish boys. It stayed at or near the top through the 1980s and ranks second or third of all time, depending on the dataset. The charts follow it in Israel, the United States and the wider world.

    Charts of the name's use in Israel, the United States and worldwide, with first attestations by community.

    11 · "From Moses to Moses there arose none like Moses"

    Bearers of the name

    The line above is engraved on Maimonides' grave. From the prophet Moses to Moshe ben Maimon, it says, no one compared. Since late antiquity the name has been carried by rabbis and generals, poets and physicists, and, as Musa, by conquerors, imams and kings.

    12 · Our reading, and yours

    Verdict

    We still think the name is most likely Semitic. The new research moved us in both directions, so here is how.

    One finding helps the Egyptian side. Late Bronze Age cuneiform spells the same Egyptian ms both ways, with sh in Amarna letter 20 and with s in Amarna letter 49. Gary Rendsburg and James Hoffmeier conclude that there were no fixed rules for these sounds in that period. The shin in Moshe is still a real problem for the Egyptian theory, but no longer a decisive one. The vowels and the stress still do not fit.

    Two findings help the Semitic side. Hoffmeier once defended the Egyptian derivation. Since 2022, writing with Rendsburg, he inclines toward a Semitic origin, related to the Ugaritic word mṯ (the ṯ is a "th" sound), "boy." And Isaiah 63:11 may hold a fourth use of the verb, where one modern Jewish translation reads Moshe as "The One who pulled a precious people out [of the water]."

    Against all this, BDB still calls the Egyptian origin probable, and the proposed relatives of the Hebrew verb in other Semitic languages mostly mean "wipe" or "wash." So our numbers stay where they were, at 55 percent Semitic, 30 percent Egyptian ms and 15 percent for the rest. That third band holds the other proposals, among them Aaron Adair's late-Egyptian (Demotic) one, and the chance that the origin cannot be recovered at all. It combines the two smaller bands of our earlier reading, 10 and 5 percent. These are judgment calls, not measurements.

    The short answer. Moshe means "the one who draws out." Whether that was the first meaning or a Hebrew reading of an Egyptian "child," the tradition has used it as a statement about what he would do.
